intro: New York lies at the mouth of the Hudson River on the Atlantic coast of the United States, a city of five boroughs on islands and the shore round one of the world’s great natural harbours. Manhattan, the long island at its heart, is a grid of avenues and numbered streets lined with skyscrapers. The Dutch founded it as New Amsterdam, millions of immigrants came in through its harbour, and today it is the largest city of the United States and a world capital of money, theatre, art and fashion.

overview: Manhattan is an island about 21 kilometres long and at most 4 wide, between the Hudson River and the East River. In 1811 the city laid a grid over it: twelve avenues running north and south, and numbered streets crossing them from east to west, with only Broadway, the old Indian trail, running across at a slant. Downtown, at the southern tip, is the old city and Wall Street; Midtown, between about 34th and 59th Street, is the second business district, the one with the tallest towers and most of the sights; Central Park lies to the north of it.

Instant New York takes you round Midtown: down Seventh Avenue through Times Square, along 34th Street to the Empire State Building, up Fifth Avenue past the Public Library and Bryant Park, along 42nd Street past Grand Central to the Chrysler Building, and back along 49th Street by Rockefeller Center. In the game, as in the real city, most of the cars are yellow cabs, and most of the avenues are one-way.
setting: New York grew round its harbour, where the Hudson meets the Atlantic, sheltered behind Staten Island and Long Island. Only the Bronx lies on the mainland; Manhattan and Staten Island are islands, and Brooklyn and Queens lie on the west end of Long Island. Hundreds of bridges and tunnels tie them together, and Manhattan’s hard bedrock is what lets its skyscrapers stand so tall and so close.

The climate is one of hot, humid summers and cold winters, with snowstorms now and then that bring the city to a halt. Rain falls in every season, and in late summer and autumn the tail of a hurricane sometimes reaches it.

history.title: New Amsterdam
text: The Lenape people lived on the island they called Mannahatta when Giovanni da Verrazzano sailed into the harbour in 1524 and Henry Hudson sailed up the river in 1609. The Dutch West India Company set up a trading post here in 1624, and two years later Peter Minuit is said to have bought Manhattan from the Lenape for goods worth 60 guilders.

New Amsterdam grew round a fort at the southern tip, with a wall across the island where Wall Street runs today. In 1664 an English fleet took it without a fight, and it was renamed New York after the Duke of York.

history.title: The port of a continent
text: After the War of Independence New York was briefly the capital of the United States, and George Washington took his oath as the first president on Wall Street in 1789. In 1811 the city laid out the grid of streets that would cover Manhattan, long before the houses reached that far north.

The Erie Canal, opened in 1825, linked the harbour with the Great Lakes, and New York became the biggest port of America. Millions of immigrants from Ireland, Germany, Italy and Eastern Europe came in through it, from 1892 through Ellis Island, and crowded into the tenements of the Lower East Side.

history.title: Greater New York
text: In 1898 Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx and Staten Island joined into one city. The first subway line opened in 1904, Grand Central Terminal in 1913, and the city grew upwards: the Woolworth Building, the Chrysler Building and in 1931 the Empire State Building were each the tallest building in the world.

After the Second World War the United Nations made its home on the East River, and New York became the centre of the art world and of finance. In the 1970s the city nearly went bankrupt and many of its streets were run down, but it recovered in the 1990s.

history.title: Since 2001
text: On 11 September 2001 terrorists flew two planes into the twin towers of the World Trade Center, which collapsed, killing nearly 3,000 people. One World Trade Center, the tallest building in the Western Hemisphere, opened on the site in 2014.

Since then the city has given more of its streets back to people on foot and on bikes: Broadway through Times Square was closed to cars in 2009, bike lanes run along the avenues, and old railway lines and piers have become parks, such as the High Line on the West Side.

today: New York is the largest city of the United States, with about 8.5 million people, more than a third of them born abroad. Wall Street and Midtown are home to banks, the stock exchanges, the big media companies and the headquarters of the United Nations, and the subway carries millions of people a day, all night long.

Visitors come for the view from the Empire State Building and the Top of the Rock, the museums on Fifth Avenue, the shows of Broadway, the lights of Times Square, Central Park and the ferry to the Statue of Liberty. In Midtown the streets are full from morning to midnight: office workers, tourists, food carts on the corners and yellow cabs honking in the traffic.
